metadata.title: Central Limit Theorem: Means Become Bell-Shaped
metadata.subject: Statistics
metadata.objective: Show a fixed non-normal population and a sampling distribution of means that narrows into a bell shape as n grows.
misconceptions: The central limit theorem needs normal data to start
expectedUnderstanding: The raw population can be skewed and non-normal.
The distribution of sample means centers near the population mean.
Its spread narrows as n grows.
The raw data does not itself become normal.

primitives.text: Raw population: skewed, not normal (stays fixed)
Distribution of sample means for sample size n
Dashed line = population mean. Larger n narrows the sample-mean distribution toward a bell; raw data stays skewed.

checkpoints.title: The raw data can be non-normal
checkpoints.body: The top histogram is skewed: most mass sits on the left, with a longer right tail. The central limit theorem does not require the raw population to be normal.

checkpoints.title: Averages, not raw observations
checkpoints.body: The bottom bars are sample means. Each mean averages n independent draws from the skewed population. The top histogram and the bottom histogram describe different things.

checkpoints.title: Increase n and watch the shape
checkpoints.body: Drag n upward. The middle bars grow and the outer bars shrink, so the sampling distribution becomes taller in the center and narrower in the tails: it approaches a bell shape.

checkpoints.title: The raw data stays skewed
checkpoints.body: The top bars never change. Averaging reduces the variability of the mean, but it does not turn individual observations into a normal distribution.

checkpoints.title: Center and spread
checkpoints.body: The dashed line marks the population mean, and the sampling distribution stays centered there. Its spread shrinks roughly with 1/sqrt(n) as n grows.

narration.text: The raw population is skewed; the central limit theorem does not need normal data.
The bottom histogram shows sample means, one bar per value of the mean.
As n grows, the sample-mean distribution narrows and becomes bell-shaped.
The raw data does not become normal; only the distribution of means changes shape.

fallback.text: The top histogram shows a skewed, non-normal population that stays fixed. The bottom histogram shows the distribution of sample means, each computed from n draws. When n is small, the sample-mean distribution is broad and still reflects the skew. As n grows, the middle bars rise and the outer bars fall, so the sampling distribution becomes narrower and approaches a bell shape centered near the population mean. The spread shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(n). The raw population does not become normal: averaging changes the distribution of the mean, not the individual observations. The central limit theorem therefore does not require normal raw data.

accessibility.alt: Top histogram: four fixed skewed raw-data bars. Bottom: seven sample-mean bars around a dashed mean line. Increasing n makes the lower bars peak in the middle and shrink at the sides, forming a bell while the top stays fixed.
